1Implicit functions, level surfaces and the differential

A relation f(x,y)=c (or f(x1​,…,xn​)=c) defines a function implicitly; geometrically it is a level curve or level surface, on which f keeps the same value. Examples are equipotential surfaces and isotherms. On a level surface the total differential df=fx​dx+fy​dy+… is zero, and that single fact gives every implicit-differentiation formula. The differential is also used in substitution and error estimates.

Key terms and definitions

Implicit function. A function given by a relation f(x,y)=c (for example x3y+3xy2=3) rather than by a formula y=g(x). S004·3 · T004a 00:00:18
Level surface (level curve). The set where z=f(x,y)=c (or f(x1​,…,xn​)=c). Examples: equipotential surfaces, isotherms. The cylinders x2+y2=c and the spheres x2+y2+z2=c are layers, one for each c. S004·4 · T004a 00:02:35 · T004a 00:03:29
Total differential. For z=f(x,y): dz=fx​dx+fy​dy. For z=f(x1​,…,xn​): dz=fx1​​dx1​+⋯+fxn​​dxn​. The total derivative is also called the differential. S004·3 · S004·4 · T004a 00:02:04
“The total derivative is also called the differential. The differential is used in integration by substitution and in approximation. It is also useful to calculate the Errors in approximation.” S004·4
“If z represents a level surface, i.e. if z=f(x,y)=c, then dz=0. The total derivative is also called the differential.” S004·4

Important points and why

  1. Integration by substitution uses the differential: with t=x2, dt=2xdx, so ∫ex2xdx=21​∫etdt. ESA ★ transcript only T004a 00:07:57 · T004a 00:08:29
  2. Errors and approximations, another application of the differential, come at the end of the unit. ESA ★ transcript only T004a 00:08:47
  3. Restriction to remember: the formula needs z=f(x,y) to be a constant (a level curve). Move everything to one side first: f(x,y)=c or f(x,y)=0. ESA ★★★ T004a 00:01:49 · T004a 00:02:04
  4. Level surfaces in physics: equipotential surfaces (constant potential) and isotherms (constant temperature). ESA ★ T004a 00:02:35
  5. x2+y2=c gives a family of cylinders (layers), and x2+y2+z2=c1​ a family of spheres about the origin: c1​=0 is the origin, c1​=1 the unit sphere, larger c1​ larger spheres. ESA ★ S004·4 · T004a 00:03:10 · T004a 00:03:42
  6. f(x1​,…,xn​)=c is still a level surface for n>3, even though it cannot be plotted; its total differential is still 0. ESA ★ T004a 00:04:34
short-note recap
A relation f(x,y)=c or f(x1​,…,xn​)=c defines an implicit function; geometrically it is a level curve or level surface (isotherm, equipotential surface), e.g. the cylinders x2+y2=c or spheres x2+y2+z2=c. On it f does not change, so its total differential df=fx​dx+fy​dy+⋯=0. The differential is also used in substitution in integrals and in error estimates.

2Implicit differentiation in two variables

For f(x,y)=c, y is a function of x and dxdy​=−fy​fx​​. The branch diagram shows why. The formula replaces long product-rule differentiation, gives tangent lines through the slope, and handles relations such as (cosx)y=(siny)x. Combined with a composite function, it gives du/dx along a curve.

Key terms and definitions

“Setting dxdz​=0 leads to a simple computation formula for implicit differentiation: fx​⋅1+fy​dxdy​=0.” S004·5

Formulas

E2.1 · Implicit differentiation, two variablesESA ★★
f(x,y)=c ⟹ dxdy​=−fy​fx​​,fy​=0
givesSlope of the level curve at a point.appliesfy​=0 at the point.noteFrom df=fx​dx+fy​dy=0. Slide 004·4 prints the fraction upside down.
S004·5 · S004·6 · T004a 00:06:36 · T003b 00:10:33
E2.2 · Tangent line at a pointESA ★★
y−y0​=m(x−x0​),m=dxdy​​(x0​,y0​)​
givesEquation of the tangent to the curve at (x0​,y0​).applies(x0​,y0​) on the curve.noteThrough the origin: y=mx.
S004·7 · T004a 00:14:25
E2.3 · Derivative of a constant power and a variable powerESA ★★
dxd​ax=axlna,dxd​xn=nxn−1
givesThe two rules needed for (cosx)y and (siny)x.appliesIn a partial derivative, the other variable is a constant.noteln needs a positive argument: cosx>0, siny>0.

Graphs and diagrams

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. Differentiating an implicit relation directly needs the product rule on every term, and the right-hand constant gives 0. ESA ★★ S004·3 · T004a 00:00:48
  2. The formula dy/dx=−fx​/fy​ gives the same answer and is far easier when f is complicated. ESA ★★ T004a 00:06:19 · T004a 00:06:36
  3. There are two ways to solve “find dy/dx”: differentiate both sides directly, or use −fx​/fy​. Both are accepted. ESA ★★ S003·27 · T003b 00:10:33
  4. The slope dy/dx at a point gives the tangent line y−y0​=m(x−x0​). ESA ★★ S004·7 · T004a 00:12:01
  5. For (cosx)y=(siny)x the result needs cosx>0 and siny>0, because of the logarithms. ESA ★ T004a 00:18:12
  6. Implicit and composite together: if u=tan(x2+y2) and x2−y2=2, use the relation to eliminate y (or find dy/dx) before differentiating. ESA ★★ CW U1 P16 · CW U1 P18
Why is dy/dx=−fx​/fy​?
Along the curve f(x,y)=c the value of f does not change, so df=fx​dx+fy​dy=0. Divide by dx: fx​+fy​dxdy​=0. The branch diagram (Figure G2.1) shows the same sum.
S004·4 · S004·5 · T004a 00:07:39
Why is the level-curve slope −fx​/fy​ and not −fy​/fx​ (as printed on slide 004·4)?
From fx​+fy​y′=0 you get y′=−fx​/fy​. Test it on x2+y2=5 at (2,1): −fx​/fy​=−2x/(2y)=−2, which matches differentiating directly; −fy​/fx​ would give −1/2.
added for clarityS004·4 · S004·5
Exam trap. Slide 004·4 prints dy/dx=−fy​(x,y)/fx​(x,y). The correct formula is dy/dx=−fx​/fy​. added for clarity S004·4
Exam trap. In (cosx)y, with respect to x it is a power (y(cosx)y−1(−sinx)); with respect to y it is an exponential ((cosx)ylncosx). S004·8 · T004a 00:16:02

short-note recap
An implicit function is given by a relation f(x,y)=c, a level curve. Along it df=fx​dx+fy​dy=0, so dxdy​=−fy​fx​​ (fy​=0). Direct differentiation of both sides gives the same result. The slope at (x0​,y0​) gives the tangent y−y0​=m(x−x0​); e.g. xey+yex=0 has tangent x+y=0 at the origin.

3Implicit functions of three variables

A relation f(x,y,z)=0 is a level surface and makes z a function of x and y. Holding y fixed gives ∂z/∂x=−fx​/fz​. Holding z fixed gives ∂y/∂x=−fx​/fy​. Denominators must be non-zero, the point must lie on the surface, and second derivatives must remember that z still depends on x and y.

Key terms and definitions

Implicit function of three variables. f(x,y,z)=0 with z (or y) regarded as a function of the remaining variables; the other variables are intermediate variables. S004·6 · T004a 00:09:05
“Let f(x,y,z)=0 be the equation of an implicit function of three variables x,y,z. Suppose y and z are functions of x, then f is a function of one independent variable x and y, z are intermediate variables.” S004·6

Formulas

E3.1 · Implicit differentiation, three variablesESA ★★
f(x,y,z)=0:∂x∂z​=−fz​fx​​,∂y∂z​=−fz​fy​​  (fz​=0);∂x∂y​=−fy​fx​​  (fy​=0)
givesPartial derivatives of the implicitly defined variable.appliesHold y constant for zx​; hold z constant for yx​.noteExtends to any number of variables.
S004·6 · S003·26 · T004a 00:10:23 · T003b 00:09:29

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. For f(x,y,z)=0, x and y are independent, so dz alone has no meaning; find the partials zx​, zy​. ESA ★★ T004a 00:09:38
  2. For ∂z/∂x treat y as constant; for ∂y/∂x treat z as constant. ESA ★★ S004·6 · S004·9 · T004a 00:19:00
  3. The formula avoids separating z from a messy equation such as x3y2+3xyz+sin(ez)=c. ESA ★ T004a 00:10:55
  4. Check that the given point satisfies f=0 before substituting. ESA ★★ added for clarity S004·9 · T004a 00:18:39
Exam trap. The lecture works problem 3 at (1,0,2) and gets 0 for both derivatives, but (1,0,2) is not on z3+xy−y2z=6 (it gives 8). Use the slide's point (0,1,2): ∂y/∂x=1/4, ∂z/∂x=−1/11. added for clarity S004·9 · T004a 00:20:47

short-note recap
For f(x,y,z)=0, z is a function of x and y: ∂x∂z​=−fz​fx​​ (hold y), ∂y∂z​=−fz​fy​​, and ∂x∂y​=−fy​fx​​ (hold z), provided the denominators are non-zero. Check that the point lies on the surface. For second derivatives, remember that z still depends on x,y.

4Composite functions and the chain rule

If u=f(x,y) and x,y depend on two new variables, u is a composite function of the new variables. Knowing this chain fixes the chain-rule formula: one term per intermediate variable. The exam questions in this topic prove identities that hold for any outer function f.

Key terms and definitions

Chain rule (several variables). If z=f(x,y) is a bivariate function and x, y are functions of two or more independent variables u, v, then ∂u∂z​=∂x∂z​∂u∂x​+∂y∂z​∂u∂y​ and ∂v∂z​=∂x∂z​∂v∂x​+∂y∂z​∂v∂y​. S003·13 · T003a 00:21:07
The chain of a problem. The list of dependencies, e.g. “u depends on x,y; x,y depend on r,t; so u is a composite function of r,t”. Knowing it fixes which chain-rule formula to write. T004b 00:02:31
“We can define chain rule for a function of two or more independent variable: If z=f(x,y) is a bivariate function and x,y are functions of two or more independent variables say u,v then we can find the partial derivative of z with respect to u and v.” S003·13

Formulas

E4.1 · Chain rule, two intermediate variablesESA ★★★
∂u∂z​=∂x∂z​∂u∂x​+∂y∂z​∂u∂y​,∂v∂z​=∂x∂z​∂v∂x​+∂y∂z​∂v∂y​
givesPartial derivatives of a composite function.appliesz=f(x,y), x=g(u,v), y=h(u,v).noteAll derivatives are partial, because everything depends on two variables.
S003·13 · S003·14 · T003a 00:21:07
E4.2 · Chain rule, three intermediate variablesESA ★★★
∂x∂v​=∂r∂v​∂x∂r​+∂s∂v​∂x∂s​+∂t∂v​∂x∂t​
givesOne term per intermediate variable.appliesv=f(r,s,t), each of r,s,t a function of x,y,z.noteA term is 0 when that intermediate variable does not contain x.
S003·15 · T003a 00:23:10
E4.3 · Function of one intermediate variableESA ★★
u=f(r), r=x2+y2+z2​ ⟹ ∂x∂u​=f′(r)∂x∂r​=f′(r)rx​
gives∂u/∂x in terms of f′(r).appliesu depends on x,y,z only through r.

Important points and why

  1. It is essential to know the chain given in the problem: what depends on what. The formula follows from it. ESA ★★★ T004b 00:02:31
  2. When u is a composite function of r,θ (or s,t), eliminate x and y from the final answer: you must know why you substitute. ESA ★★★ T004b 00:07:52 · T004b 00:10:28
Why does u=f(x−y,y−z,z−x) give ux​+uy​+uz​=0?
Each argument is a difference whose derivatives sum to zero: for r=x−y, rx​+ry​+rz​=1−1+0=0. Adding the three chain-rule expressions gives fr​(0)+fs​(0)+ft​(0). In words: moving x, y, z by the same amount changes none of the arguments.
added for clarityESA Jan-24 s2 1d
Why do the chain-rule answers keep fr​ and fθ​?
The outer function f is unknown, so its partial derivatives cannot be computed; only the inner derivatives (rs​=t, θs​=s/s2+t2​, …) can.
S003·17 · T003a 00:26:28

short-note recap
If u=f(x,y) and x,y depend on s,t (or r,θ), u is a composite function of s,t, and us​=fx​xs​+fy​ys​, ut​=fx​xt​+fy​yt​: one term per intermediate variable. Write the chain first. If f is unknown, keep fx​,fy​ as symbols. Eliminate x,y from the final answer. Standard results: ux​+uy​+uz​=0 for f(x−y,y−z,z−x); xux​+yuy​+zuz​=0 for f(x/y,y/z,z/x).

5Composite functions in polar coordinates

Most of the class 004 problems use x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ (or the reverse, r=x2+y2​, θ=tan−1(y/x)). Compute the inner derivatives once, apply the chain rule, then eliminate x and y. Functions of x2+y2 alone give uθ​=0; tan−1(y/x) gives uθ​=1.

givesThe inner derivatives for polar problems.appliesr=x2+y2​, θ=tan−1(y/x).noteSo ux​=fr​rx​−fθ​r2y​ and uy​=fr​ry​+fθ​r2x​ for u=f(r,θ).

Graphs and diagrams

Flowcharts

Important points and why

  1. Functions of x2+y2 alone (e.g. sin(x2+y2), ex2+y2) have ∂u/∂θ=0 in polar coordinates, since x2+y2=r2 does not involve θ. ESA ★★ added for clarity S004·10 · S004·13 · S004·14
  2. tan−1(y/x) is exactly θ in polar coordinates, so ∂u/∂θ=1. ESA ★★ added for clarity S004·15
Exam trap. Do not stop with x and y still in an answer that should be in r,θ or s,t. T004b 00:07:52

givenu=sin(x2+y2), x=rcost, y=rsint; find ut​.

checku=sinr2 does not involve t at all.

step 3Substitute: −2r3cosθsin2θ+r3cos3θ=r3cosθ(3cos2θ−2).
answer∂θ∂u​=r3cosθ(3cos2θ−2)+r(3θ2sinθ+θ3cosθ)

givenu=u(x,y), x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ.
step 1ur​=ux​cosθ+uy​sinθ.

CW U1 P15
short-note recap
With x=rcosθ, y=rsinθ: xθ​=−rsinθ, yθ​=rcosθ; with r=x2+y2​, θ=tan−1(y/x): rx​=x/r, ry​=y/r, θx​=−y/r2, θy​=x/r2. Functions of x2+y2 alone have uθ​=0, tan−1(y/x) has uθ​=1, and ux2​+uy2​=ur2​+uθ2​/r2.

Eight past ESA papers were checked: UE22MA141A Dec 2023, Jul 2023 and May 2024, and UE23MA141A Jan 2024 sets 1–4 and June 2024. In scope: one implicit-function question (Jan 2024 set 3 Q1.d, 6 marks) and five composite-function (chain rule) questions (Jan 2024 set 1 Q1.d and set 2 Q1.d, 5 marks; set 3 Q1.b, set 4 Q1.b and June 2024 Q1.a, 6 marks). Polar-coordinate problems and tangent lines to implicit curves were not asked in these papers; they are computed in class and in CW problems 15–18. Total-derivative and rate problems (class 003) are left out.

Known gaps, conflicts and corrections

  1. Slide 004·4 prints dy/dx=−fy​/fx​ for a level curve. It should be −fx​/fy​, as slide 004·5's branch diagram and slide 004·6 show.
  2. Slide 004·3's numerator is hard to read in the rendering. The correct dy/dx for x3y+3xy2=3 is −3y(x2+y)/(x(x2+6y)).
  3. In the lecture (T004a 00:18:39) problem 3 of deck 004 is worked at the point (1, 0, 2), giving 0 for both derivatives. That point is not on z3+xy−y2z=6 (it gives 8). The slide's point (0, 1, 2) is on the surface and gives ∂y/∂x=1/4, ∂z/∂x=−1/11.
  4. The lecture says the differential is “minus zx​ by zy​” (T004a 00:07:05); that expression is the slope dy/dx, not the differential. The differential is df=fx​dx+fy​dy.
  5. Slides 004·4, 004·6 and 004·7 show screenshots from online 3-D graphers (calculus7.com, intmath.com). They are redrawn as Figures G1.1 and G2.2 rather than copied.
  6. The same class 004 content is also in the classes 003–004 pack; problems and answers are identical in both.
  7. Transcript recognition errors were corrected silently: “Gosteep” → cos θ, “composive” → composite, “dou dita” → ∂θ, “sec y” → zy​, “psi x” → sin x.
